Johann Funck
yoh'hahn foonk
n. (1518–1566; Königsberg court preacher and chronicler, Osiander's son-in-law, beheaded in the ducal crisis)
Funck, a German surname from Funke, a spark; Johann from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Johann Funck studied at Wittenberg, came to Königsberg in 1547, married Andreas Osiander's daughter, and became Duke Albert's court preacher and the chief voice of the Osiandrist party in Prussia. Osiander had taught that a man is justified by the indwelling righteousness of Christ rather than by a righteousness imputed to him, and Funck defended it with the duke's favour behind him for nearly twenty years, while the Samland clergy and the university were driven out or silenced. He also meddled far outside the pulpit, in the duke's finances and in the business of the Polish crown, alongside the adventurer Paul Skalich. In 1566 the Prussian estates, with Polish backing, arrested the court party; Funck was tried at Kneiphof and beheaded. His own chronicle of the world, the Chronologia, outlived him. The dictionary records him as a plain warning: “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a courtier as one who attends the court of a prince, and one who flatters to please; a faction as a party in political society combined for a common interest; and a canker as an eating or corroding sore.

expand to see more

COURTIER, n. One who attends or frequents the courts of princes; one who courts or flatters in order to please.

FACTION, n. [L. factio.] A party, in political society, combined or acting in union to oppose the government, or another party; dissension; tumult.

CANKER, n. A corroding or eating sore; a disease that eats away the flesh; anything that corrupts or consumes by degrees.

PRIDE, n. Inordinate self-esteem; an unreasonable conceit of one's own superiority.

JUSTIFY, v.t. [L. justus.] To prove or show to be just; in theology, to pardon and clear from guilt, and to accept as righteous on account of the merits of the Savior.

Key Scripture

1Co 10:12 — "Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall."

Pro 16:18 — "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall."

2Ti 2:17 — "And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;"

Gal 2:16 — "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified."

Modern Corruption

Königsberg court preacher and Osiander's son-in-law, who held the duke's ear for the Osiandrist doctrine of justification until the estates arrested the court party and beheaded him in 1566.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The entry does, however, have to resist two bad verdicts. The one makes Funck a martyr of conscience killed by a mob of politicians; the other makes him a swindler whose theology was a cover. Neither is honest. He appears to have believed Osiander's doctrine; he also used a prince's favour to silence men who answered it, and traded on the pulpit for influence in matters that were none of his business. He was executed without a trial worth the name, and that was a crime against him. The doctrine he defended was still wrong.

The principle to recover is the one the Osiandrists lost, and it is the whole hinge of the gospel: the righteousness by which a sinner is accepted is Christ's own, reckoned to him, and not a quality worked up inside him — “Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). A false teaching does not stay in the study; Paul uses a surgeon's word for it, “And their word will eat as doth a canker” (2Ti 2:17). And a favoured man near a throne should read his own position with the proverb open: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek gangraina (G1044), a gangrene or canker; Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify or declare righteous.

Greek gangraina (G1044) — a gangrene, an eating sore; “will eat as doth a canker”, 2 Timothy 2:17.

Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, to justify; Galatians 2:16.

Greek pipto (G4098) — to fall; “take heed lest he fall”, 1 Corinthians 10:12.

Hebrew ga'on (H1347) — pride, arrogance, swelling; Proverbs 16:18.

Hebrew shever (H7667) — a breaking, destruction; Proverbs 16:18.

Usage

"“Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12) — court preacher at Königsberg from 1547."

"“And their word will eat as doth a canker” (2Ti 2:17) — nearly twenty years of Osiandrist ascendancy in Prussia."

"“Pride goeth before destruction” (Pro 16:18) — tried and beheaded at Kneiphof, 1566."
